title: Making up parts and learning from Redman and Edward Cuffy
summary: With few second trombone parts he invents his own; Redman, who knew every instrument, taught him and Cuffy helped him practice.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So I sang, went on and sang with the band and I got so, just like we was speaking it before, I got so that I didn't have a lot of second trombone parts, you know.
So I listened to the band and I started

making up parts, you know. So one night I'm sitting there, you know, just calmly and I didn't have no part to something, you know, and Don Redmon was a big kidder but I didn't know it at that time. He got a lot of kick out of me, you know, being young and I didn't know. So he come over to me and he said, "Hey, you, why aren't you playing in there?" And I said, "Well, Mr. Redmon, I haven't got a part to that." He said, well, "Play in there anyway." So I grabbed up my horn and I made up a part anyway and played. But it was a great experience and I learned a lot from Edward Cuffy, too, because
Cuppy was a trombone player, right?

Yes. I used to practice with him and I learned a lot from Mr. Redmon because Mr. Redmon knew every instrument in the band and if you didn't know, he would take your horn and show you. He could. You know, he knew just how to write because he knew how every position on the trombone, how it laid, trumpet, alto saxophone, and all that. I've seen him take a saxophone player's horns and they have a tough passage and he would watch them finger it and he would tell them no. He said, "You finger it this way," you know, and it would be a faster way of fingering, an easier way. I've seen him do that, you know.
And then that's when I started to playing the second trombone and I started to really learn how to play low notes, and I love low notes, you know. And I learned a lot from Mr.
Redman to that extent, you see. He was like a teacher.
